title: Which additive noises preserve median-based skewness?
shortTitle: Adding noise can flip which tail is heavier
oneLine: A counterexample to Hunter's conjecture, a classification of noise laws, and the gamma, beta and Lévy cases
abstract: Hunter (2026) called a distribution right van Zwet skewed when, at every distance from its median, the right tail carries at least as much probability as the left, and conjectured that independent log-concave laws with this property keep it under addition. This candidate shows that the conjecture fails, and determines how completely. A triangular variable plus independent uniform noise is an exact counterexample; for that input, right skewness survives uniform noise exactly up to half-width (3 − √3)/4 ≈ 0.317. Only a point mass preserves skewness in general: for every nonconstant noise law, with no moment assumption, some right-skewed input with a positive, real-analytic, strongly log-concave density has a sum with the noise that is skewed in neither direction. A single such input fails for every positive weighted sum of two or more independent copies of itself and after adding Gaussian noise of any variance. The proofs rest on a characterisation of symmetry through uniform smoothings, which also gives an identity along the population Huber location path and a distribution-free procedure that certifies opposite tail imbalances from a sample. Complete proofs are given for three cases Hunter supported by simulation: every gamma law, beta laws with b ≥ a ≥ 1 (essentially contained in Sato's analysis of Pearson laws) and the Lévy law; an appendix settles weak limits and same-median mixtures. Limits: the counterexamples concern the exact definition, and the Gaussian-noise tail reversals are far out and tiny; no positive preservation result is proved; the certificate has no power comparison. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 15-page paper with a context-first introduction, written proofs of every result, limits, open problems and an AI-use statement. Three Python programs accompany it: check_hunter.py checks the counterexample, the 0.317 threshold and the atomic example in exact rational arithmetic; check_families.py gives 40-digit numerical diagnostics for the gamma, beta and Lévy section (checks, not proofs); huber_certificate.py runs the sample certificate on deterministic controls. A clean replay in Python's optimised mode reproduced the recorded outputs; changing 1/162 to 1/161 makes check_hunter.py fail; Linux CI reruns all three.

keyResults: Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 (proof): Beta(1,2) plus independent uniform noise on [−1, 1] has median 1/3 and tail imbalance +1/162 at distance 2/3 and −1/1296 at distance 3/2, so it is neither right nor left van Zwet; with uniform noise on [−r, r] right skewness survives exactly for r ≤ (3 − √3)/4 ≈ 0.317.

Theorem 3.1 (proof): a law with a positive continuous density is symmetric if and only if all its uniform smoothings are skewed in one direction, equivalently if the slopes of the smoothed densities at their medians share one sign.

Theorem 4.1 (proof): for every nonconstant noise law, with no moment assumption, some right van Zwet input with a positive, real-analytic, strongly log-concave density gives a sum that is neither right nor left van Zwet.

Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.2 (proof): one such input fails for every positive weighted sum of two or more independent copies of itself and after adding Gaussian noise of any variance; the tail reversals lie far from the median.

Proposition 6.2 (proof): every gamma law, every Beta(a, b) with b ≥ a ≥ 1, and the Lévy law are right van Zwet; the beta case is essentially contained in Sato (1995). Corollary 7.1: a distribution-free certificate of opposite tail imbalances with error at most α.

Credit and limits: Hunter (definition in this form, median inequality, conjecture, closure questions), van Zwet, Sato, Tan–Wang–Zhou, Thompson–Forbes–MacEachern–Peruggia, Reeve after Massart. The counterexamples concern the exact definition; no positive preservation result; no power comparison for the certificate.
